newsitem.title: EL SALVADOR: In El Salvador, death squads again draw fire.
newsitem.headline: In El Salvador, death squads again draw fire.

text.p: The Roman Catholic Church in El Salvador warned on Wednesday that death squads that terrorised leftist activists in the 1980s are now targeting street criminals and gang members.

Some 40 vigilante murders in 1997 have been attributed to death squads, the shadowy, right-wing paramilitary groups that became a hallmark of El Salvador's 12-year-long civil in which 75,000 people were killed.
The war ended in 1992, with leftist guerrillas laying down their arms and becoming a legal political party.
Tutela Legal, the archbishop's highly influential human rights office, said the reactivated death squads today are attacking a different enemy.
"It's the same squad structure that is now active and violting human rights," Maria Julia Hernandez, director of Tutela Legal, told Reuters in an interview.
"We think they are death squads because of the way in which they move around," Hernandez said, referring to unregistered cars with tinted windows, traits of the death squads of the 1980s.
Three police officers have been arrested on accusations they belonged to death squads that killed common criminals and youth gang members in the capital of San Salvador and the city of Santa Ana.
In the 1980s, human rights groups including Tutela Legal linked death squads to government security forces.
The director of the National Civilian Police, Rodrigo Avila, denied that death squads exist within the police force, telling reporters the arrest of the officers was "an isolated case."

Tutela Legal said in a report that the arrested police officers are tied to an underground group called the Black Shadow, a group accused of killing about 20 presumed street criminals in 1994 in the city of San Miguel, about 85 miles (140 km) east of San Salvador.
All of the 16 suspects arrested in the San Miguel case have been released and charges were dropped.
The auxiliary bishop of San Salador, Gregorio Rosa Chavez, on Sunday denounced the recent wave of vigilante killings as recalling "the worst moments of the death squads."
